title: Why enzymes stop working when they get too hot
examples: What is the optimum temperature for enzymes?

explain.say: Have you noticed that when you have a high fever, doctors want to cool you down quickly? It is partly to protect your enzymes, the tiny helpers that run every reaction in your body. Let's see what heat does to them.

draw.text: Why enzymes stop working when they get too hot

explain.say: Look at the left of the curve. When it is cold, molecules move slowly, so the enzyme and its substrate bump into each other less often. The reaction is slow. Can you guess why food lasts longer in a fridge?

Now the top of the hill. As it warms up, molecules move faster and meet more often, until the best temperature, called the optimum. For most enzymes in your body it is about 37 °C. What is your body temperature?

See the steep drop? Too much heat shakes the enzyme so hard that its active site changes shape. The substrate no longer fits. We say the enzyme is denatured, and it does not come back. Can you think of a fried egg that cannot be unfried?
So enzymes work best at their own optimum. Brilliant! Wow fact: bacteria in hot springs have enzymes that love about 70 °C, and scientists use one of them to copy DNA in labs.

faq.q: Why are enzymes slow in the cold?
faq.a: At low temperatures molecules have less energy and move slowly, so enzymes and substrates collide less often. The enzyme is not damaged, just slow.
asks: Tell me about the cold end

faq.a: The optimum is the temperature at which an enzyme works fastest. For most human enzymes it is about 37 °C, our body temperature.
Denatured means the enzyme's shape, including its active site, has been permanently changed by heat or extreme pH, so the substrate can no longer fit.
A very high body temperature, above about 40 °C, can start to disturb the shapes of some proteins and enzymes and the cells that rely on them, so doctors work to bring it down.
asks: Is a fever bad for enzymes?

faq.q: Do all enzymes have the same optimum?
faq.a: No. Enzymes from bacteria in hot springs can work best near 70 °C or more, while enzymes in Arctic fish work well near 0 °C.

facts: Most human enzymes have an optimum temperature of about 37 °C.
Taq polymerase, from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, works best at about 72 °C and is used to copy DNA in PCR.

quiz.say: What happens to an enzyme's active site when it is denatured?
quiz.show: What happens to an enzyme's active site when it is denatured?

options.show: It gets bigger and works faster
options.say: It gets bigger and works faster

quiz.why: Heat breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.

wrong.1: A denatured enzyme stops working; it does not speed up.
wrong.2: Denaturing is permanent damage, not a rest.

quiz.say: Why is a reaction slow at 5 °C?
quiz.show: Why is a reaction slow at 5 °C?

options.show: Molecules move slowly and collide less
options.say: Molecules move slowly and collide less

quiz.why: In the cold, molecules have little energy, so fewer collisions happen.

wrong.0: Cold slows enzymes but does not denature them.
wrong.2: The substrate is still there; it just meets the enzyme less often.
